title: Pulmonary Function Tests: Obstruction, Restriction, Diffusion, Quality
bottomLine: Interpret PFTs in sequence: confirm test quality, identify obstruction, use lung volumes to confirm restriction, then use diffusion capacity and clinical context to refine the differential. A low FVC on spirometry alone does not prove restrictive lung disease.
recognize: Obstruction is suggested by a reduced FEV1/FVC relative to appropriate reference limits; bronchodilator response supports variable airflow disease but is not the sole asthma criterion.
True restriction requires reduced total lung capacity; low DLCO can reflect emphysema, ILD, pulmonary vascular disease or anemia depending on context.
differentiate: Low FVC may reflect restriction, air trapping, obesity, neuromuscular weakness or poor effort.
A normal spirometry result does not exclude exercise-induced asthma, early ILD or pulmonary vascular disease when the clinical probability remains meaningful.
assessment: Review symptoms, smoking/occupational exposure, atopy, medications, prior imaging, neuromuscular disease and whether the patient could perform reproducible manoeuvres.
workup: Confirm acceptability/reproducibility, interpret spirometry with current reference equations, obtain lung volumes/DLCO or bronchoprovocation when the unanswered question requires them.
management: Use the physiologic pattern to guide disease-specific workup rather than treating the PFT label itself; refer unexplained restriction, reduced diffusion or complex mixed physiology to respirology.
medicationSafety: Bronchodilator-withholding instructions must fit the test purpose and remain safe for the patient; do not withdraw essential therapy in an unstable patient for elective testing.
redFlags: Disproportionately reduced DLCO with pulmonary vascular concern
counselling: Explain that effort and technique affect test quality and that an uninterpretable test should be repeated, not blamed on the patient.
followUp: Repeat testing only when it can confirm diagnosis, document meaningful progression or change treatment.
examTrap: Diagnosing restriction from a low FVC without lung-volume confirmation.
oneLinePearl: Spirometry suggests restriction; total lung capacity proves it.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society Pulmonary Function Testing resources

title: Thoracentesis: Diagnose the Effusion, Drain Safely
bottomLine: Thoracentesis is diagnostic when pleural fluid cause is uncertain and therapeutic when a sizable effusion is causing symptoms. Use ultrasound-guided site selection, review bleeding/respiratory risk, stop if the patient deteriorates, and send fluid studies matched to the differential rather than an indiscriminate panel.
recognize: Unilateral, atypical, febrile or unexplained effusions often need diagnostic sampling; a classic bilateral HF effusion improving with diuresis may not need immediate tap.
Therapeutic drainage can improve dyspnea but does not replace treatment of infection, malignancy or heart failure.
differentiate: Complicated parapneumonic effusion/empyema often requires chest-tube drainage rather than repeated simple thoracentesis.
Pneumothorax, bleeding, vasovagal events and re-expansion pulmonary edema are important complications.
assessment: Review indication, ultrasound anatomy, oxygenation, hemodynamics, anticoagulants/antiplatelets, platelet/coagulation context, mechanical ventilation and ability to cooperate.
workup: Use pleural protein/LDH and targeted cell count, glucose/pH, culture, cytology or other testing according to suspected infection/malignancy/other cause.
management: Use sterile ultrasound-guided technique by appropriately trained clinicians; monitor symptoms and vital signs during/after drainage and escalate suspected pneumothorax, bleeding or respiratory deterioration.
medicationSafety: Periprocedural anticoagulant decisions are individualized to drug, indication, bleeding risk and local protocol; do not apply one universal INR/hold rule.
counselling: Explain the diagnostic purpose, expected discomfort and symptoms requiring immediate reporting during or after the procedure.
followUp: Review every pleural-fluid result and imaging finding through to the underlying diagnosis; symptom relief alone is not closure.
examTrap: Performing repeated therapeutic taps on an empyema without definitive drainage/source control.
oneLinePearl: Thoracentesis can sample or relieve fluid; the pleural diagnosis still needs an owner.

title: Allergic Rhinitis and Sinusitis: Allergy, Viral Illness, or Bacterial Pattern?
bottomLine: Allergic rhinitis is an inflammatory exposure-related syndrome; most acute rhinosinusitis is viral. Reserve antibiotics for a compatible bacterial pattern or complication risk, and use intranasal corticosteroid/allergen strategies rather than repeated systemic antibiotics for chronic nasal symptoms.
recognize: Sneezing, itch, watery rhinorrhea and exposure/season pattern support allergic rhinitis.
Bacterial sinusitis is more likely with persistent symptoms without improvement, severe onset or clear double-worsening rather than coloured mucus alone.
differentiate: Uncomplicated viral URI commonly causes facial pressure and purulent-appearing discharge.
Unilateral obstruction/bleeding, orbital signs, severe headache/neurologic findings or recurrent focal disease require another diagnosis.
assessment: Assess duration/pattern, allergens, asthma, fever/severity, dental symptoms, medication use, pregnancy, immune status and red flags.
workup: Routine imaging is not needed for uncomplicated acute rhinosinusitis or typical allergic rhinitis; CT/endoscopy/allergy testing is selected for chronic/refractory/complicated disease.
management: Use allergen avoidance, saline and intranasal corticosteroid/appropriate antihistamine therapy for rhinitis; provide symptomatic care for viral sinusitis and evidence-based antibiotics only when bacterial criteria are met.
medicationSafety: Avoid prolonged topical decongestant use because rebound congestion can occur; systemic decongestants require cardiovascular/pregnancy consideration.
counselling: Explain why green/yellow mucus does not by itself mean antibiotics are needed and teach correct intranasal-spray technique.
followUp: Reassess persistent/recurrent symptoms for asthma, anatomy, allergy or alternative diagnoses rather than repeating empiric antibiotics indefinitely.
examTrap: Prescribing antibiotics because nasal discharge is coloured on day four of an otherwise uncomplicated viral illness.
oneLinePearl: Sinusitis becomes bacterial by clinical course and severity—not by mucus colour.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada antimicrobial stewardship principles

title: Acute Bronchitis vs Pneumonia: Who Needs Imaging or Antibiotics?
bottomLine: Most acute bronchitis is viral and does not benefit from antibiotics. Suspect pneumonia when vital signs, oxygenation, focal lung findings, frailty/immune risk or clinical trajectory suggest lower-respiratory parenchymal infection; use chest imaging when it can meaningfully confirm or change that decision.
recognize: Cough can persist for weeks after viral bronchitis; sputum colour does not prove bacterial infection.
Pneumonia concern rises with fever, tachypnea, hypoxemia, focal crackles/bronchial breathing or systemic illness.
differentiate: Asthma/COPD exacerbation, PE, HF and pertussis can mimic prolonged bronchitic cough.
Older/immunocompromised patients can have pneumonia with muted fever or leukocytosis.
assessment: Assess vitals, oxygenation, work of breathing, focal exam, age/frailty, immune status, aspiration risk, COPD/asthma and symptom trajectory.
workup: Avoid routine chest radiography for low-risk bronchitis with normal vitals/exam; obtain imaging when pneumonia probability or alternate dangerous diagnosis is meaningful.
management: Provide symptomatic care and safety-netting for bronchitis; treat confirmed/strongly suspected pneumonia according to Canadian/local guidance and severity.
medicationSafety: Unnecessary antibiotics cause adverse effects, C. difficile and resistance; routine bronchodilator/corticosteroid use is not indicated unless underlying airway disease warrants it.
redFlags: Failure to improve/worsening after initial course
counselling: Set expectations for cough duration and give specific return precautions rather than using antibiotics as reassurance.
followUp: Reassess worsening or persistent symptoms and investigate recurrent focal pneumonia or cancer/TB risk.
examTrap: Giving antibiotics for coloured sputum when the patient has normal vitals, oxygenation and lung examination.
oneLinePearl: Bronchitis is usually a cough syndrome; pneumonia changes the vitals, lungs or trajectory enough to earn a different pathway.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada respiratory/antibiotic stewardship resources

title: CAP vs HAP: Setting, Severity, and Resistance Change the Plan
bottomLine: Community-acquired and hospital-acquired pneumonia differ in pathogen/resistance risk and empiric treatment. Confirm a compatible clinical/radiographic syndrome when feasible, assess severity and aspiration/immune context, then choose the narrowest appropriate regimen with a reassessment/de-escalation plan.
recognize: CAP develops outside hospital/recent healthcare exposure; HAP develops after hospitalization and carries different resistant-organism probabilities.
Older adults may present with delirium/functional decline rather than fever; aspiration risk changes organism/complication thinking but does not automatically require broad anaerobic coverage.
differentiate: Colonization/positive respiratory culture is not pneumonia without compatible illness.
Pulmonary edema, PE, atelectasis, drug pneumonitis and malignancy can mimic infiltrates.
assessment: Assess oxygenation, hemodynamics, mental status, respiratory rate, comorbidities, recent antibiotics/hospitalization, aspiration, immune status and local resistance risk.
workup: Use chest imaging and targeted cultures/microbiology according to severity and setting; obtain blood/sputum cultures selectively when results are likely to alter management.
management: Treat CAP with guideline/local first-line therapy matched to severity/comorbidity; HAP requires hospital protocol and resistant-pathogen risk assessment. Narrow or stop therapy as microbiology/clinical data permit and ensure source/complication management.
medicationSafety: Renal/hepatic dosing, QT risk, C. difficile risk and drug interactions matter; avoid importing broad HAP regimens into ordinary CAP without risk evidence.
counselling: Explain expected recovery and return precautions; vaccination/smoking/aspiration prevention become part of recurrence prevention after stabilization.
followUp: Review culture results and antibiotic duration, and reassess persistent focal findings/symptoms rather than automatically extending antibiotics.
examTrap: Using the same empiric antibiotic approach for community pneumonia and new hospital-acquired pneumonia regardless of resistance risk.
oneLinePearl: Pneumonia treatment begins with where it was acquired, how sick the patient is, and what resistance risk is real.

title: Lung Cancer Screening: High-Risk and Asymptomatic Only
bottomLine: Lung cancer screening uses low-dose CT in asymptomatic people who meet a validated high-risk program pathway. Hemoptysis, unexplained weight loss or a suspicious known nodule is not a screening problem—it requires diagnostic evaluation.
recognize: Canadian provincial programs use smoking/risk criteria and organized LDCT pathways; exact eligibility and funding vary by province/territory.
Screening can reduce lung-cancer mortality in appropriately selected high-risk populations but also causes false positives and overdiagnosis.
differentiate: Screening is for people without symptoms; known nodule surveillance and symptomatic suspected cancer follow diagnostic pathways.
A standard chest x-ray is not the evidence-based lung-cancer screening test.
assessment: Assess age, smoking duration/intensity, quit status, COPD, prior cancer/family history, fitness for potential treatment, symptoms and patient values.
workup: Refer through the current provincial/territorial organized LDCT risk-assessment program where available; do not invent one Canada-wide age/pack-year rule.
management: Use shared decision-making about benefits/harms, smoking cessation and program follow-up; abnormal screening CTs must follow the standardized nodule pathway.
medicationSafety: No medication prevents the need to investigate a suspicious symptomatic presentation; avoid repeated antibiotic trials for persistent red-flag symptoms.
counselling: Explain that screening is active prevention for high-risk people who feel well, not a shortcut for evaluating symptoms.
followUp: Track every screening result and next LDCT/diagnostic action to completion; re-assess smoking risk according to the current program.
examTrap: Sending a patient with hemoptysis into a routine annual screening pathway instead of diagnostic assessment.
oneLinePearl: If symptoms suggest lung cancer, stop calling the test screening.
sourceBasis: Cancer Care Ontario Ontario Lung Screening Program 2026

title: Occupational Lung Disease: The Exposure History Is Diagnostic Data
bottomLine: Work-related lung disease includes asthma but also pneumoconioses, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, toxic inhalation and occupational COPD/cancer risk. Build an exposure timeline by job, task and protective controls, match physiology/imaging to the exposure, and intervene early because continued exposure can cause irreversible disease.
recognize: Silica, asbestos, coal/metal/mineral dusts, isocyanates, mould/organic antigens and fumes have distinct respiratory risks.
Symptoms improving away from work support work-related disease but chronic fibrotic disease may no longer fluctuate with exposure.
differentiate: Occupational asthma is variable airway disease; pneumoconiosis/ILD often produces restrictive physiology/imaging; irritant exposure can cause acute inhalation injury or chronic airway disease.
assessment: Record every job/task, duration, material, ventilation/PPE, co-worker illness, symptom timing, smoking and latency—not just the current job title.
workup: Use spirometry/full PFTs, chest imaging/HRCT and exposure-specific testing or occupational/respirology referral according to suspected disease.
management: Reduce/remove harmful exposure, treat the lung disease and coordinate occupational health/workplace accommodation/compensation pathways according to jurisdiction.
medicationSafety: Escalating inhalers or steroids while hazardous exposure continues is incomplete treatment; immunosuppression requires infection exclusion in ILD phenotypes.
redFlags: Inability to avoid a serious exposure
counselling: Explain that documentation of exposure and objective changes can be important for both health and workplace protections.
followUp: Trend lung function/exposure status and close specialist/occupational recommendations.
examTrap: Treating progressive restrictive disease while never asking what dusts, fumes or antigens the patient encounters at work.
oneLinePearl: In occupational lung disease, the job-task history can be as important as the CT scan.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society occupational/environmental respiratory principles

title: Pulmonary Nodule Follow-Up: Risk, Morphology, Growth, Ownership
bottomLine: An incidental pulmonary nodule needs an explicit risk-based surveillance or diagnostic plan based on size, morphology, growth, prior imaging and patient cancer risk. Nodule surveillance is not lung-cancer screening, and a suspicious/symptomatic lesion should not wait for a routine surveillance interval.
recognize: Spiculation, upper-lobe location, growth, larger solid component, smoking/age and prior cancer raise malignancy risk.
Most small nodules are benign, so unnecessary PET/biopsy can cause harm.
differentiate: Organized screening uses a standardized LDCT reporting pathway; incidental nodules use the applicable nodule guideline; symptomatic suspected cancer uses a diagnostic pathway.
assessment: Review all prior imaging, smoking/exposure history, previous cancer, symptoms, immune status and whether the patient could undergo definitive treatment if malignancy were found.
workup: Use the current Canadian/local nodule pathway for surveillance interval and PET/biopsy referral; compare directly with old imaging before ordering new invasive tests.
management: Assign ownership and an exact next step/date; refer higher-risk/growing/suspicious nodules through a lung diagnostic pathway rather than repeated empiric antibiotics.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulant and pulmonary-reserve considerations matter if biopsy is planned; procedural risk must be weighed against malignancy probability.
counselling: Explain that surveillance is active management and why the chosen interval balances early diagnosis against procedural/radiation harms.
followUp: Use closed-loop tracking so no recommended CT/PET/referral is lost; document resolution or handoff of ownership.
examTrap: Using a population screening schedule for an already identified pulmonary nodule—or waiting months on routine surveillance when symptoms suggest cancer.
oneLinePearl: Every pulmonary nodule needs a risk-based plan, a date, and a named owner.
sourceBasis: Cancer Care Ontario lung screening/diagnostic pathway resources
